analysis.one_liner: Requires multinational companies to publicly disclose profits, taxes, and employees country by country.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 28-23, but it sat on the House calendar without a floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require large multinational companies registered with the SEC to file an annual public report showing, for every country where they operate, how much revenue they book, how much profit they declare, how much tax they actually pay, how many people they employ, and what assets they hold. Today, a company can book its profits in a low-tax country like Bermuda or Ireland while earning its sales in the United States, and the public cannot see the split. This disclosure would not by itself change anyone's tax bill, but it would make profit-shifting visible to investors, journalists, and tax enforcers. The bill cleared committee but never came up for a vote in the full House.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, investors, and tax enforcement. The public gets a free, machine-readable map of where each multinational books profits and pays taxes, which makes it easier to see which companies shift profits into tax havens. Investors get a clearer picture of real tax risk, and the IRS and foreign tax authorities get information that helps them challenge arrangements that move profits away from where the work happens.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each covered issuer to file annually, for every tax jurisdiction where it has entities, the revenue from related and unrelated parties, profit or loss before income tax, income tax actually paid on a cash basis, accrued tax expense, stated capital, accumulated earnings, number of full-time-equivalent employees, and net book value of tangible assets [S2][S4].

The reports must be filed in a machine-readable format and made available to the public online, so journalists, researchers, and regulators can compare profits booked in a jurisdiction with taxes paid there [S4].

The SEC must write the rules in consultation with the IRS and Treasury, conforming to U.S. or international country-by-country reporting standards, with a proposed rule within one year and a final rule within 18 months of enactment [S4].

By naming each constituent entity, its tax jurisdiction of residence, and its main business activity, the disclosure would expose cases where a subsidiary exists mainly to hold profits in a low-tax jurisdiction rather than to do business [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Large multinational companies that currently shift profits into low-tax jurisdictions would bear the cost of preparing and filing the reports, and would lose the privacy that lets them avoid public scrutiny of where they book income versus where they earn it. Tax haven jurisdictions and the accounting and advisory industry built around offshore structures would face pressure as the arrangements became visible. Consumers would largely not pay directly; the mechanism is disclosure, not a new tax or fee.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals and the offshore advisory industry

drawbacks.text: Disclosure alone does not change tax law. A company could keep shifting profits into tax havens and simply report that it is doing so; closing the gap would still require separate legislation or enforcement, and opponents could argue the bill creates paperwork without collecting a dollar of new revenue [S2][S4].

Country-by-country detail can hand competitively sensitive information to rivals and foreign governments, a cost honest supporters would acknowledge; the bill lets the SEC set the threshold and format to manage this, but the information itself is public by design [S4].
Compliance would be a real burden for the covered multinationals, and the revenue threshold is left to the SEC to set, which could determine how many companies are actually covered [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real but indirect: public visibility of profit-shifting, which supports enforcement and informed investment rather than directly raising revenue. The main costs fall on the multinationals being exposed and, to a lesser degree, on competitive privacy. On balance, a modest-cost, transparency-only bill whose value depends on regulators and lawmakers acting on what it reveals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee on a 28-23 vote and was placed on the House calendar in June 2021, but House leadership never brought it to the floor, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Cynthia Axne introduced the bill on May 7, 2021, with eight Democratic cosponsors joining at introduction [S1][S4][S5].
The House Financial Services Committee held a markup on May 12, 2021, and voted 28-23 to order the bill reported with an amendment [S6].
The committee reported the amended bill on June 8, 2021, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, the House's list of bills awaiting floor action [S6].
No floor vote ever occurred; the action record ends with the calendar placement, and the 117th Congress expired on January 3, 2023 [S1][S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational companies that shift profits into low-tax jurisdictions are better off, because the disclosure that would have made those arrangements public never happened. The offshore advisory industry serving those companies also kept its business model intact.

for.name: Rep. Cynthia Axne
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through committee; reported it amended to the House calendar.

for.name: 9 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at or shortly after introduction.

for.what_they_did: Held a markup, voted 28-23 to order the bill reported with an amendment, and reported it to the House on June 8, 2021.

sides.party_line_note: The committee approved it 28-23 with no Republican support evident in the tally, and the sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Democrats; the bill never reached a floor vote where a broader split could have shown.

industries.industry: Multinational corporations using offshore tax structures
industries.note: The bill would force public disclosure of where these companies book profits versus where they pay tax, removing the privacy that makes tax-haven strategies low-risk. Ordinary taxpayers bear the revenue loss when profits are shifted offshore, so the industry's interest in secrecy runs against the public's interest in visibility.

industries.industry: Tax haven jurisdictions and offshore financial centers
industries.note: Public country-by-country data would spotlight entities registered in low-tax jurisdictions that have little business activity there. That pressure can drive restructurings and deter profit booking in havens.

industries.industry: Accounting, tax advisory, and law firms serving multinationals
industries.note: A large part of this industry's value is designing and keeping offshore arrangements confidential. Public disclosure exposes the arrangements and raises the reputational and enforcement risk of selling them.
Only issuers in multinational groups above an SEC-set revenue threshold are covered, and they face compliance costs. Investors as a group gain better information about real tax exposure.
